title: Geometric specialization slice data and ordinary sliced comparison
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme. A geometric specialization datum consists of algebraically closed fields $A,B$, geometric points $a:\operatorname{Spec}A\to S$, $b:\operatorname{Spec}B\to S$ [def-weil-geometric-point], and an $S$-morphism $c:S_{(b)}\to S_{(a)}$ between their strict localizations [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit]. For a morphism $f:X\to S$, define $X_a=X\times_Sa$, $X_{(a)}=X\times_SS_{(a)}$, $X_{(b)}=X\times_SS_{(b)}$ [def-pc-fibre-product], with $i_a:X_a\to X_{(a)}$ induced by the canonical geometric closed point and $j_b:X_{(b)}\to X_{(a)}$ induced by $c$. For a commutative coefficient ring $\Lambda$, the sliced complex functor is $i_a^*Rj_{b,*}r_b^*$, where $r_b:X_{(b)}\to X$ is projection, using the exact constant-module inverse images and derived direct images of [def-trf-oriented-nearby-cycles]. Over a commutative scheme square $(h,g):(f':X'\to S')\to(f:X\to S)$, a compatible change of specialization consists of maps of the two geometric points over $g$, pointed maps of both strict localizations over $g$ commuting with $c,c'$, and the induced maps of the fibre and the two tubes, with their projection and $i,j$ commutation equations. Its ordinary sliced comparison is the inverse-image composition comparison for $i$, followed by the base-change mate for $j$ transposed from the actual direct-image counit, followed by the composition comparison for $r$. A geometric slice has points $(x,b,c)$ when on every oriented triple generator its inverse image at each geometric $x$ of $X_a$ is naturally the set of compatible lifts of $x,b$ with the intermediate lift extending over $S_{(a)}$ and restricting along $c$ over $S_{(b)}$. A geometric slice family assigns a geometric morphism from the étale topos of $X_a$ to $V_f$ to each $(f,a,b,c)$; the preceding point condition is a separate predicate. Its module lift is the constant-module construction, and a supplied compatible direct-image square identification induces the corresponding derived inverse-image comparison. Cohomology vanishing through $r\in\mathbf Z$ means $\mathcal H^q=0$ for every $q\le r$.
